message.content:
```bash
ffmpeg -framerate 24 -i frame_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p output.mp4
```

Adjust the input pattern to match your filenames:

- `frame_%04d.png` matches `frame_0001.png`, `frame_0002.png`, etc.
- Use `%03d` for three-digit padding, or `%d` for no padding
- Add `-start_number 0` before `-i` if your numbering starts at 0 instead of 1

Useful options:

- `-crf 18` — quality control (lower = better, 18–23 is typical; default is 23)
- `-r 24` after the input — output frame rate (only needed if it differs from input)
- `-vf "scale=trunc(iw/2)*2:trunc(ih/2)*2"` — auto-fixes odd dimensions, since yuv420p requires even width/height

Example with quality and odd-size handling:

```bash
ffmpeg -framerate 24 -i frame_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -pix_fmt yuv420p -vf "scale=trunc(iw/2)*2:trunc(ih/2)*2" output.mp4
```

If your frames are named arbitrarily rather than numbered sequentially, use a glob pattern instead: `-pattern_type glob -i "*.png"` (note: glob sorts lexically, so `frame10.png` comes before `frame2.png`).

The ffmpeg command to convert PNG frames to MP4 at 24fps:

```
ffmpeg -framerate 24 -i frame_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p output.mp4
```

Key points:
- `-framerate 24` sets the input frame rate (how fast to read the images)
- `-i frame_%04d.png` is the input pattern — assumes files like frame_0001.png, frame_0002.png, etc.
- `-c:v libx264` uses H.264 codec
- `-pix_fmt yuv420p` ensures compatibility with most players (QuickTime, browsers)
- Optionally `-crf 18` or similar for quality control
- `-start_number 0` if frames start at 0
